It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific combination of single-pass fragment shader execution with dynamic branching, transmittance-based early termination, and dithered starting positions [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim contains three specific technical features: 1) 'single-pass fragment shader execution', 2) 'dynamic branching', and 3) 'dithered starting positions'. Source [S1] explicitly supports 'dithered starting positions' (notes: 'Apply dithering to starting position to hide aliasing') and implies single-pass execution via the description of the 'Main rendering loop' in the fragment shader. However, Source [S1] does not mention 'dynamic branching' as a distinguishing feature; it describes a fixed loop structure with early termination based on a threshold, which is a standard optimization but not necessarily 'dynamic branching' in the context of distinguishing the technique from siblings. Source [S2] describes a technique that uses early termination based on transmittance ('terminates early if transmittance drops below a threshold'), which supports the 'transmittance-based early termination' part of the claim. However, Source [S2] does not mention 'dithered starting positions' or 'single-pass' execution in the provided text (it uses Three.js which often implies a specific pipeline, but the code snippet doesn't confirm the 'single-pass' nature as a distinguishing feature against siblings in the same way S1 does). Crucially, the claim attributes all these features to a single entity ('It'). The evidence shows S1 has dithering and S2 has transmittance-based termination. Neither source explicitly claims to have *all* these features combined as a unique distinguishing signature. Specifically, 'dynamic branching' is not supported by the evidence in S1 (which uses a fixed loop) or S2 (which uses a fixed loop with break conditions). Therefore, while some facts are present in the evidence, the specific combination and the 'dynamic branching' aspect are not fully supported or are attributed to different sources/methods, making the claim only partially supported by the provided text.
supported
